_comment: The critic's eval set: pairs of contact sheets whose ranking a human has
already settled, so that a change to the prompt, the model or the protocol
is answered with a number instead of an opinion. Run it with
profiles/visual/creative/critic-eval.sh — live only, and it costs real money.
Every path is relative to profiles/visual/creative/eval/. Per pair:
id      — what the table calls it.
better  — the sheet the human ranked higher. The runner promotes this one
as the CHAMPION, because that is the role the reigning render
plays in a real round.
worse   — the sheet the human ranked lower; run as the CHALLENGER. null
means 'the same file again', which is how the identical-sheets
pair is written.
challenger — optional, 'worse' (default) or 'better': which side is
presented as the challenger. Flip it to author a pair whose
expected answer is `better`.
expect  — what the calibrated gate should return for the challenger:
better | worse | tie.
Only pairs whose expect is `better` or `worse` are enforced (a wrong
answer there exits non-zero): those are the ones a human judged outright.
A `tie` pair is measured and reported — a concordant strong verdict on one
is information, not a regression.
The sheets are the real artefacts from PR #1's live demo of the wall:
six frames of the same shot, 3x2, under the 500 KB the Read tool
recompresses above.
refs — optional directory of reference-board PNGs (relative to this
file), handed to the critic exactly as the gate hands VISUAL_REFS. Measure
with the board the gate will use: without one the judge grades raw taste,
which is not what the gate acts on. --refs on the command line overrides.

pairs.note: The shipped DOM city against the rejected 'city life' canvas render. The owner's verdict was unambiguous and instant; the un-calibrated critic answered `worse` when the DOM sheet was labelled the champion and `worse` again when the labels were swapped, which is the status-quo bias this protocol exists to remove. The pair that has to come out right.

The ?world=canvas parity port of the same city: near-equal by eye, and the pair that produced `worse`/`fail` on one run and `better`/`pass` on the next from identical inputs. A concordant `better` or `worse` here is tolerated and reported rather than failed — what would be a regression is the two orders disagreeing every time.

The same sheet twice. There is no picture to prefer, so anything but `tie` is the judge preferring a position over an image — the cheapest possible detector of the bias, and the one that must never regress.
